title: The BASS Principle for Predictable Maxillary Sinus Bone Augmentation: A Conceptual Narrative Review
content: Maxillary sinus floor elevation is common, yet newly formed bone remains unpredictable even when the Schneiderian membrane is intact and the immediate radiograph shows a well-shaped dome. Single-cause explanations do not account for this variability. Sinus augmentation differs from ridge augmentation: it creates a closed, air-filled, non-sterile compartment in which osteogenesis proceeds centripetally from the surrounding bony walls rather than from a vascularized defect bed. We therefore define the BASS principle, comprising Bone contact area, Angiogenesis, Stability of Space, and Safe healing. Bone contact area sets the osteogenic source and diffusion distance; angiogenesis sets the rate at which cells and nutrients reach the graft centre; stability of space preserves the container against intranasal pressure, graft resorption and micromotion; safe healing keeps it biologically undisturbed until mineralization is complete. The four domains are coupled, not additive: failure of any one is sufficient to make the outcome unpredictable. We map each domain onto measurable preoperative cone-beam computed tomography variables, intraoperative manoeuvres and recognizable failure phenotypes, and propose a workflow spanning case selection, surgical design and follow-up. BASS is a preventive design framework rather than a complication rescue algorithm; its thresholds require prospective validation.
